passages.title: The Lost Dog
passages.text: Jay saw the dog on Monday, on his way home from school. It was sitting by the gate of the park, with its head on its paws. It had no collar and no lead, and it looked cold and thin. Jay stopped and held out his hand. The dog sniffed it, then licked his fingers. Its tail began to thump on the path. Jay did not know what to do. He could not just leave it there, but he could not take it home either. His mum had said no pets, many times. In the end he sat on the wall and shared the rest of his lunch. The dog ate every crumb and then rested its chin on his knee. When Jay got up to go, the dog got up too. It followed him all the way down the hill and over the bridge. At the corner shop, Mrs Patel came out to see what was going on. She looked at the dog for a long time. Then she said that her brother had lost a dog just like this one, a week ago, when it ran off in the storm. She rang him on the shop phone. Ten minutes later a van pulled up, and a tall man jumped out. The dog went wild. It barked and spun round and jumped up at the man. The man was laughing and crying at the same time. Before he left, he shook Jay's hand and told him to come and visit any time he liked.

passages.title: Storm on the Island
passages.text: The wind had been rising all afternoon. By the time Mia and her grandad had pulled the boat up the beach, the sky over the sea was dark grey, almost black. Grandad looked at the clouds and said the ferry would not run tonight. That meant they were on the island until the morning, just the two of them and the old stone cottage. Inside, Mia lit the lamps while Grandad got the fire going. Rain began to hit the windows, softly at first and then in hard bursts that made the glass shake. The cottage had stood on that hill for more than a hundred years, Grandad said, and it had seen far worse storms than this one. Mia tried to believe him. They ate soup and bread by the fire and played cards until the lamps began to flicker. Then there was a crash outside, loud enough to make them both jump. Grandad took the torch and opened the door a crack. The wind pushed in at once, cold and wet and full of the smell of the sea. In the beam of the torch they could see that the shed roof had blown off and landed in the garden. Nothing could be done about it in the dark. Grandad shut the door and pushed a chair against it. Mia did not sleep much that night. But when the grey light came, the wind had dropped, the sea was calm, and far away she could hear the horn of the first ferry.

passages.title: The Night Bus
passages.text: Leo had never been on the night bus on his own before. His sister was meant to meet him at the stop, but she had sent a message to say she was stuck at work. So there he was, at ten past nine, with his football boots in a bag and his phone on six per cent. The bus was nearly empty. An old man was asleep near the front, and two women were talking quietly at the back. Leo sat by the window and watched the dark streets slide past. He counted the stops in his head. He had to get off at the ninth one, next to the big supermarket. After a while the lights outside began to look the same, and Leo started to worry. Had that been the fifth stop or the sixth? He could not remember. His phone buzzed once and then the screen went black. Leo felt his heart speed up. He made himself breathe slowly, the way his coach told the team to before a penalty. Then he stood up, walked to the front and asked the driver. The driver was a cheerful woman with a bright red scarf. She smiled and said the supermarket was the stop after next, and that she would shout when they got there. Leo sat down on the front seat to wait. When the bus stopped, she called out to him and waved. Leo jumped off, and there was his sister, running across the car park to meet him.

passages.title: Bees in the School Garden
passages.text: Last spring, our school started a garden club. At first it was just a few of us digging weeds out of an old flower bed behind the sports hall. Then Mr Ahmed had a better idea. He wanted to plant flowers that would bring bees into the garden. Bees need flowers because they feed on the sweet nectar inside them. As a bee moves from flower to flower, it also carries a fine yellow dust called pollen. This helps plants to make seeds and fruit. Without bees and other insects, many of the plants we eat would struggle to grow. We planted lavender, foxgloves and a patch of wild flowers along the fence. For weeks nothing much seemed to happen. Then, on a warm afternoon in June, the whole bed was humming. There were fat, fuzzy bumblebees and smaller, thinner bees that moved so fast they were hard to follow. We sat very still on the grass and watched them. Mr Ahmed showed us how to tell some of them apart by their colours and the shape of their bodies. He also told us that bees will not usually sting if you leave them alone and do not wave your arms about. Now we have a chart on the classroom wall, and each week someone counts the bees for ten minutes and writes down what they see. We are hoping that next year, with more flowers, the numbers will go up again.

passages.title: The Trial
passages.text: Sam's hands were shaking as he laced up his boots. The trial for the town team started in five minutes, and there were at least forty other players on the pitch already. Most of them looked older than him, and some looked a lot bigger. A coach in a blue jacket blew a whistle and called everyone over. He split them into four groups and gave each group a set of coloured bibs. Sam was in green. The first drill was simple passing in pairs. Sam's first pass went too far and rolled off the pitch, and he felt his face go hot. He told himself to slow down and look at the ball. After that, his passes were clean and firm. Next came a short game, six against six. Sam played on the left, which was not his best side, but he did not complain. Near the end of the game, the ball broke loose in the middle. Sam got to it first, turned away from a defender and slipped a pass through to the striker, who scored. A few of his team mates clapped him on the back. When it was over, the coach read out a list of names for a second trial next week. Sam stood at the back and tried not to look hopeful. The list went on and on, and he had almost given up when he heard it. Sam Okafor. He did not cheer. He just grinned all the way home.

passages.title: Under the Old Bridge
passages.text: Nobody used the old bridge any more. A new road had been built further down the river, and the stone bridge had been left to the ivy and the pigeons. That was why Priya was surprised to see fresh footprints in the mud on the path beneath it. They were small, smaller than hers, and they led right into the dark space under the arch. She called out, but no one answered. The only sound was the water slapping against the stones. Priya almost turned back. Then she remembered the poster she had seen in the window of the post office. A boy from the village had gone missing that morning. He was seven, and he had been wearing a yellow coat. Priya switched on the torch on her phone and stepped under the arch. The air was cold and smelled of wet earth. At first she saw nothing but moss and old leaves. Then the light caught a flash of yellow in a gap between two fallen stones. A small boy was curled up there, fast asleep, with a muddy rabbit in his arms. Priya knelt down and gently woke him. He told her that the rabbit had run away from his garden and he had chased it all the way to the river. Then he had got tired and could not find the way back. Priya held his hand and walked him up the path to the road, where she rang the number on the poster.
